power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background.
Acquired brain injury (ABI) is a leading cause of long-term disability in adults.
In Canada, while advances in acute care and inpatient rehabilitation have improved survival, many people living with ABI experience persistent challenges following discharge.
This can include reduced self-efficacy, mental health difficulties, and decreased participation in daily life.
Community-based supports remain fragmented and difficult to access.
Peer support, or mentorship provided by people with lived experience of ABI, has shown promise in improving outcomes in neurological and chronic conditions.
However, peer support interventions for ABI are rarely described in sufficient detail to enable replication or implementation.
Objective.

To describe the development, theoretical foundations, core components, and delivery of Peers Actively Involved in Rehabilitation (PAIR), a structured, community-based peer support intervention for adults living with ABI.
Methods.

This paper provides a detailed description of PAIR using the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR), informed by principles from the Guidance for Reporting Intervention Development studies (GUIDED).
Data sources include co-creation with people with lived experience and community partners, feasibility research, intervention manuals, and operational procedures.
Discussion.
PAIR integrates lived experience knowledge into rehabilitation through structured peer support worker training, individualized matching, and flexible delivery embedded within community organizations.

By transparently documenting development and delivery, this paper supports replication, adaptation, and future evaluation, and contributes to strengthening person-centred, community-based rehabilitation for adults living with ABI.

Acquired brain injury (ABI), including traumatic and non-traumatic etiologies such as traumatic brain injury, stroke, anoxic injury, and infection, is a leading cause of long-term disability among adults worldwide [1].
text.formatted: Acquired brain injury (ABI), including traumatic and non-traumatic etiologies such as traumatic brain injury, stroke, anoxic injury, and infection, is a leading cause of long-term disability among adults worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Advances in acute medical management and inpatient rehabilitation have improved survival and early recovery.
However, many people living with ABI experience persistent physical, cognitive, emotional, and psychosocial challenges that extend well beyond discharge from formal rehabilitation services [2].
text.formatted: However, many people living with ABI experience persistent physical, cognitive, emotional, and psychosocial challenges that extend well beyond discharge from formal rehabilitation services <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Given these long-term consequences, ABI has been conceptualized as a chronic health condition requiring ongoing, community-based support rather than time-limited impairment-focused care [3].
text.formatted: Given these long-term consequences, ABI has been conceptualized as a chronic health condition requiring ongoing, community-based support rather than time-limited impairment-focused care <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: In many countries, health services for ABI remains disproportionately concentrated in acute and specialized inpatient settings, with limited continuity of rehabilitation support following discharge.
Research indicates substantial gaps in care once people with ABI return to the community [4, 5].
text.formatted: Research indicates substantial gaps in care once people with ABI return to the community <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: People with ABI describe inadequate access to psychosocial supports, difficulties navigating health and social services, and limited opportunities for individualized rehabilitation aligned with personal goals and priorities [6].
text.formatted: People with ABI describe inadequate access to psychosocial supports, difficulties navigating health and social services, and limited opportunities for individualized rehabilitation aligned with personal goals and priorities <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: These gaps in supports are associated with reduced self-efficacy, poorer mental health, decreased participation, and lower quality of life for people living with ABI [4, 5].
text.formatted: These gaps in supports are associated with reduced self-efficacy, poorer mental health, decreased participation, and lower quality of life for people living with ABI <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: Peer support has emerged as a promising approach to address these persistent gaps in care [7].
text.formatted: Peer support has emerged as a promising approach to address these persistent gaps in care <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Peer support involves mentorship provided by people with lived experience of a condition to others who are earlier in their journey with the condition [8, 9].
text.formatted: Peer support involves mentorship provided by people with lived experience of a condition to others who are earlier in their journey with the condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr">9]</ref>.

text.text: In neurological and chronic conditions (e.g., spinal cord injury, stroke), peer support has been associated with improvements in self-efficacy, emotional wellbeing, coping, and quality of life, and may complement clinician-led rehabilitation by addressing experiential and relational dimensions of recovery [9, 10].
text.formatted: In neurological and chronic conditions (e.g., spinal cord injury, stroke), peer support has been associated with improvements in self-efficacy, emotional wellbeing, coping, and quality of life, and may complement clinician-led rehabilitation by addressing experiential and relational dimensions of recovery <ref type="bibr">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: For adults living with ABI specifically, qualitative and mixed-methods studies suggest that peer support facilitates normalization of experience, reduces social isolation, supports adjustment to life after injury [8].
text.formatted: For adults living with ABI specifically, qualitative and mixed-methods studies suggest that peer support facilitates normalization of experience, reduces social isolation, supports adjustment to life after injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Emerging evidence also suggests potential indirect benefits for family members and caregivers through improvements in self-efficacy and access of support beyond the family [8].
text.formatted: Emerging evidence also suggests potential indirect benefits for family members and caregivers through improvements in self-efficacy and access of support beyond the family <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: There is substantial heterogeneity in reporting peer support interventions for ABI, with limited description of core components, peer support worker training, fidelity, and theoretical foundations [9].
text.formatted: There is substantial heterogeneity in reporting peer support interventions for ABI, with limited description of core components, peer support worker training, fidelity, and theoretical foundations <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref>.

text.text: As such, peer support interventions are difficult to replicate, implement, and scale-up.
Additionally, given the diversity of outcomes included, it is difficult to compare and synthesize outcomes across studies [9, 11].
text.formatted: Additionally, given the diversity of outcomes included, it is difficult to compare and synthesize outcomes across studies <ref type="bibr">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: Standardization of reporting, not necessarily of intervention content, has been identified as a key priority for advancing peer support as an evidence-informed component of ABI rehabilitation [8] [9] [10].
text.formatted: Standardization of reporting, not necessarily of intervention content, has been identified as a key priority for advancing peer support as an evidence-informed component of ABI rehabilitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: There has been increasing recognition that effective rehabilitation interventions, particularly those addressing long-term disability, must be grounded in person-centred and patient-partnered approaches [12, 13].
text.formatted: There has been increasing recognition that effective rehabilitation interventions, particularly those addressing long-term disability, must be grounded in person-centred and patient-partnered approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: Co-creation and co-design are processes that meaningfully engage people with lived experience as partners across intervention development, implementation, and evaluation; they are associated with improved relevance, acceptability, and sustainability of rehabilitation programs.

Involving people with lived experience of ABI is particularly important given the heterogeneity of rehabilitation trajectories and life contexts, and the historically limited involvement of this population in shaping the services intended to support them [14].
text.formatted: Involving people with lived experience of ABI is particularly important given the heterogeneity of rehabilitation trajectories and life contexts, and the historically limited involvement of this population in shaping the services intended to support them <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: To address the discrepancy between the long-term challenges experienced after ABI, the time-limited nature of traditional rehabilitation services, as well as the limited availability of structured peer support opportunities in the community, we co-developed Peers Actively Involved in Rehabilitation (PAIR), with community partners and people with lived experience of brain injury [10, 15, 16].
text.formatted: To address the discrepancy between the long-term challenges experienced after ABI, the time-limited nature of traditional rehabilitation services, as well as the limited availability of structured peer support opportunities in the community, we co-developed Peers Actively Involved in Rehabilitation (PAIR), with community partners and people with lived experience of brain injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: The feasibility of PAIR has been previously described in a case-series pre-post study [10], indicating good recruitment rate, excellent retention, full adherence to protocol, high implementation fidelity, but limited pre-to post-intervention change on psychosocial-related outcomes (e.g., selfefficacy, resiliency).
text.formatted: The feasibility of PAIR has been previously described in a case-series pre-post study <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, indicating good recruitment rate, excellent retention, full adherence to protocol, high implementation fidelity, but limited pre-to post-intervention change on psychosocial-related outcomes (e.g., selfefficacy, resiliency).

text.text: The working alliance between the peer support worker and person receiving peer support was also reported [15], indicating that the alliance was characterised by a strong sense of mutual understanding and validation ('feeling understood'), conversations that extended beyond the injury to broader life experiences ('expanding conversations beyond injury'), and a dynamic of reciprocal growth.
text.formatted: The working alliance between the peer support worker and person receiving peer support was also reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, indicating that the alliance was characterised by a strong sense of mutual understanding and validation ('feeling understood'), conversations that extended beyond the injury to broader life experiences ('expanding conversations beyond injury'), and a dynamic of reciprocal growth.

text.text: The purpose of this paper is to describe PAIR in detail, including its development, theoretical foundations, core components, and delivery, using established reporting guidelines.
By describing PAIR, we aim to support replication, adaptation, and implementation of peer support as a meaningful component of community-based ABI rehabilitation.
Replication (TIDieR); Table 1 describes the aspects of PAIR intervention according to the TIDieR checklist.
text.formatted: Replication (TIDieR); Table <ref type="table">1</ref> describes the aspects of PAIR intervention according to the TIDieR checklist.

text.text: The reporting is informed by the Guidance for Reporting Intervention Development studies (GUIDED) to enhance transparency regarding how and why PAIR was developed, refined, and operationalized.
PAIR builds on previous research and community-based peer support initiatives.

Our community partner, Nanaimo Brain Injury Society, established a hospital-based brain injury peer support program in 2015, which was informed by approaches in amputee care, spinal cord injury, and stroke recovery.
This longstanding program offered the foundation for a research-community partnership to adapt, evaluate, and extend the intervention.
The development of PAIR was grounded in a patient-partnered, community-engaged approach that positioned people with lived experience of ABI and community members as experts and co-creators [17].
text.formatted: The development of PAIR was grounded in a patient-partnered, community-engaged approach that positioned people with lived experience of ABI and community members as experts and co-creators <ref type="bibr">[17]</ref>.

text.text: The intervention was developed iteratively through collaboration among people living with ABI, peer support workers (people who have provided peer support), leaders from community brain injury organizations, clinicians in ABI rehabilitation, and researchers.

Early development activities were informed by qualitative research exploring experiences of living with ABI [18], perceived gaps in post-discharge services [19], and reported need for peer support [6].
text.formatted: Early development activities were informed by qualitative research exploring experiences of living with ABI <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[18]</ref>, perceived gaps in post-discharge services <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[19]</ref>, and reported need for peer support <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: These findings highlighted a strong desire for peer-based support that was relational, individualized, and grounded in lived experience, particularly during the subacute and early community integration phases [5, 8].
text.formatted: These findings highlighted a strong desire for peer-based support that was relational, individualized, and grounded in lived experience, particularly during the subacute and early community integration phases <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: We (JS and JG) observed the work of community partners and people with lived experience who conducted integrated peer support programs in their local community for 8 years (Nanaimo Brain Injury Society).

During three onsite sessions and four virtual meetings, researchers and community partners had structured discussions about program operations, sustainability processes, and how to strengthen the researchcommunity partnership.

These discussions emphasized the need for a peer support model that could be expanded and integrated into other communities; meeting outcomes highlighted the need for formal training and clear operational structure, with flexibility to respond to individual needs.
Building on this foundation, PAIR was co-developed with community brain injury organizations responsible for peer support delivery (BC Brain Injury Association and Nanaimo Brain Injury Society).
These partnerships were critical in shaping the structure, training, oversight and facilitation processes, and delivery modalities of the intervention.
We co-developed and tested intervention materials, including peer support worker training content and operational procedures.
We refined these materials based on multiple rounds of feedback.

For example, JG met with two peer support workers from the community partner (Nanaimo Brain Injury Society) who provided recommendations on providing training within an online platform and offered input on the relevant health outcomes from receiving peer support.

To further refine materials, a person who previously received peer support indicated important program features to help facilitate connection with the peer support worker, including flexibility in delivery and alignment with goals and life stage.
Last, we (JG and JS) met with two community partners who were currently facilitating peer support intervention.
The community partners provided practical guidance on peer support program delivery, including oversight needs for peer support workers and strategies to ensure sustainability and communication.
Findings from our early feasibility research informed the development of recruitment and retention processes, acceptability, and perceived impact [10, 15].
text.formatted: Findings from our early feasibility research informed the development of recruitment and retention processes, acceptability, and perceived impact <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: Further feedback of the feasibility research was obtained from peer support workers, participants, and community partners, which led to refinements in peer support worker training content, clarification of roles, adjustments in session frequency and duration, and development of a comprehensive standard operating procedure to facilitate consistent delivery.

For example, session frequency and duration was adjusted from eight 30-minute sessions to twelve 60-minute sessions to allow more time for relationship building, deeper conversations, and sharing of lived experiences.

Peer support worker training was expanded to include additional content on communication strategies, boundary setting, responding to emotional or complex situations, and sharing lived experience safely and effectively.
Training materials were adapted (e.g., presentation slides, written material) to be aphasia friendly with the assistance of a speech language pathologist and a person with aphasia.
Role descriptions were clarified to better distinguish the responsibilities of peer support workers, coordinators, and clinical partners, including guidance around communication and oversight.

Aligned with our earlier findings on pairing participants with peer support workers, recruitment and matching processes were refined by incorporating participant goals, shared lived experience characteristics, and logistical considerations (e.g., availability) [15].
text.formatted: Aligned with our earlier findings on pairing participants with peer support workers, recruitment and matching processes were refined by incorporating participant goals, shared lived experience characteristics, and logistical considerations (e.g., availability) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Finally, a detailed standard operating procedure was developed to support program fidelity while allowing continued changes, such as safety plans and communication protocols.
PAIR is grounded in social learning theory, which posits that people learn new behaviours, coping strategies, and perspectives through observing and interacting with others [20].
text.formatted: PAIR is grounded in social learning theory, which posits that people learn new behaviours, coping strategies, and perspectives through observing and interacting with others <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Peer support workers serve as credible role models, demonstrating strategies for navigating life with ABI.
They acknowledge the ongoing challenges individuals face, while also offering a sense of hope.

The intervention also draws on theories of resiliency, which is understood as a dynamic process involving cognitive, emotional, and behavioral capacities that support adaptation in the face of adversity [21].
text.formatted: The intervention also draws on theories of resiliency, which is understood as a dynamic process involving cognitive, emotional, and behavioral capacities that support adaptation in the face of adversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[21]</ref>.

text.text: For people living with ABI, resiliency has been associated with improved mental health, participation, and quality of life [22].
text.formatted: For people living with ABI, resiliency has been associated with improved mental health, participation, and quality of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref>.

text.text: PAIR is designed to promote resiliency peer support that models adaptive coping strategies, validates lived experiences, and fosters hope for life after ABI.
Principles of person-centred care have further informed PAIR [23] [24] [25].
text.formatted: Principles of person-centred care have further informed PAIR <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[25]</ref>.

text.text: These principles emphasize expertise of lived experience and collaborative relationships.

Within PAIR, this is operationalized through the inclusion of peer support workers with brain injury and partnerships with leaders from community brain injury programs, whose experiential knowledge offers a credible form of expertise complementing clinical perspectives.
Evidence suggests that incorporating programs including shared lived experience can foster trust, engagement, and hope.
Rather than focusing on remediating an impairment, PAIR prioritizes participant-identified goals and values.

This focus is important because person-centred goal-setting has been associated with improved engagement and more meaningful rehabilitation outcomes by aligning interventions with content that matters to the individual.

In contrast, a sole emphasis on impairment remediation may not translate into improved participation or quality of life, particularly in ABI where long-term adaptation and identity reconstruction are central [26].
text.formatted: In contrast, a sole emphasis on impairment remediation may not translate into improved participation or quality of life, particularly in ABI where long-term adaptation and identity reconstruction are central <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[26]</ref>.

text.text: As such, PAIR focuses on goals of the individual with peer-delivered support.
Key materials supporting PAIR were co-created and tailored for various partners involved in program delivery.
Descriptions are as follows.
For peer support workers, we co-developed tools with community partners and people with lived experience to promote intervention fidelity.
Fidelity indicators were aligned with PAIR's theoretical framework, as described above, such as offering hope and sharing lived experience (see Appendix A).

We also co-created standardized peer support worker training curriculum, co-developed with community partners and aligned with Peer Support Canada core competencies [27] (see Appendix B for description of peer support session content).
text.formatted: We also co-created standardized peer support worker training curriculum, co-developed with community partners and aligned with Peer Support Canada core competencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[27]</ref> (see Appendix B for description of peer support session content).

text.text: We created infographics to assist peer support workers to initiate conversations, comply with safety protocols, and understand their role (see Appendix C for safety plan).
For research staff, we created a comprehensive standard operating procedure.

This document guides the intervention processes such as eligibility screening and recruitment, participant matching processes, risk management considerations (e.g., safety plan), and communication processes (e.g., email templates).
The document also outlines research practices such as outcome assessment, data collection and management, fidelity monitoring, and adherence to ethical requirements.

For clinical partners involved in screening of potential participants, we created eligibility checklists for ease of screening participants in clinical settings and infographics to share with potential participants, if needed.
We also created a secure online data sharing system for partners to share the contact information of potential participants.
For potential participants, we developed infographics to explain the peer support intervention and established a visual consent process to describe the research study (see Appendix D).
The infographic included a one-page document with a visual description of the study.
A structured, written script for researchers was developed to use during consent.

We created the process of consenting participants using visual aids, as opposed to the traditional written consent documentations, based on participant feedback gathered during our co-creation process.
Our visual documentation included relevant icons, simplified text, and step-by-step diagrams.

Participants indicated that they preferred visual materials because dense, text-heavy documents were often overwhelming and difficult to process in the context of cognitive challenges (e.g., reduced attention, memory difficulties, and slowed information processing).
To further support accessibility for participants, we created accompanying visual slides to administer outcome measures.
These visual slides displayed each question and response options with accompanying visual icons and key information bolded.
These slides were designed to reduce cognitive load by presenting one question at a time, using clear language, consistent formatting, and visual cues.

In response to additional co-creation feedback, an adapted version of the slides was developed for participants with speech and language challenges (e.g., aphasia), incorporating strategies such as simplified wording, pictorial scales, and opportunities for supported communication.

Overall, these adaptations reflect the importance of input of those with lived experience and our commitment to reducing barriers to participation and ensuring that study procedures are responsive to the diverse cognitive and communication needs of people with ABI.
PAIR consists of one-to-one peer support sessions between an adult with recent experience of ABI and a trained peer support worker with long-term lived experience of ABI.
Sessions are relational and tailored to the needs and challenges of the participants.

Common areas of discussion include adjustment to injury, coping strategies, emotional wellbeing, self-management, navigating health services, participation in meaningful activities, and rebuilding identity following injury [15].
text.formatted: Common areas of discussion include adjustment to injury, coping strategies, emotional wellbeing, self-management, navigating health services, participation in meaningful activities, and rebuilding identity following injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: A key component of the PAIR intervention is the process of matching participants with peer support workers, which is undertaken collaboratively by researchers (JG), PAIR Research Coordinator, and PAIR Community Facilitator, who provides support and encouragement to peer support workers.
Matching is guided by principles derived from co-design and feasibility work, with the aim of fostering connection and engagement between individuals [10].
text.formatted: Matching is guided by principles derived from co-design and feasibility work, with the aim of fostering connection and engagement between individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative findings from our feasibility work examined working alliance between the participant and peer support worker within PAIR.

Findings emphasized that the success of peer support relationships is not solely determined by connecting people with similar clinical and demographic characteristics, but also ensuring participants feel understood, experience mutual openness, and engage in conversations that extend beyond the injury itself.

As such, the matching process considers participant's life stage and circumstances (e.g., living alone, caring for children), demographics (e.g., age, sex, gender), goals for rehabilitation (e.g., work, social), and challenges after ABI (e.g., physical, cognitive).
Additionally, similar personal interests and relevant social or cultural factors are considered, as these can help to create rapport and connection on experiences unrelated to ABI.

The PAIR Research Coordinator and PAIR Community Facilitator also support rematching, if there is not a mutual connection after two peer support sessions; this is based on private discussions with participant and peer support worker.
Content of the peer support sessions are based on the co-created fidelity indicators, as mentioned above.
The peer support sessions follow a semi-structured approach, instead of a protocolized format.
A semi-structured format allows peer support workers to be responsive to participant needs in the moment, but have a guideline to follow during sessions.
There are 11 key aspects that are recommended in every peer support session; these relate to fostering hope, promoting self-compassion, and sharing lived experience.

There are five aspects that are not required in every session, but are recommended to be addressed at least once during the intervention; these broadly relate to discussions of the rehabilitation journey, health outcomes, and navigating health services.
Rather than prescribing session-by-session content, fidelity within PAIR adheres to core relational and ethical principles of peer support.

This approach reflects emerging consensus that effective peer support requires standardization of processes and values, rather than rigid curricular content, particularly in heterogeneous populations such as ABI [9].
text.formatted: This approach reflects emerging consensus that effective peer support requires standardization of processes and values, rather than rigid curricular content, particularly in heterogeneous populations such as ABI <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Overall, peer support workers are encouraged to draw on their lived experience in a reflective and intentional manner to emphasize mutual understanding.
Peer support workers are adults with lived experience of ABI who are more than two years post-injury.
Selection criteria emphasize readiness to support others, communication skills (can include peer support workers with aphasia), and ability to engage reflectively with lived experience.
Peer support workers were referred by local community organisations.
Peer support workers complete structured training by a research team member (JG) and receive ongoing oversight and support from the PAIR Community Facilitator.
Peer support worker training comprises of three sessions, approximately two-hours for each session.
The training was designed to prepare peer support workers with ABI to deliver the PAIR intervention within a structured and accessible approach.
Content includes an introduction to peer support with a focus on the value of lived experience as expertise and the role of the peer support worker in fostering hope, connection, and empowerment.
Peer support workers are oriented to the structure and key components of PAIR, such as tailoring conversations and sharing experiences.
Training also includes instruction on communication skills such as active listening, validation, shared storytelling, and managing conversational balance.
Additionally, strategies for adapting communication to accommodate cognitive and communication challenges are discussed (e.g., managing slowed processing and aphasia).
Peer support workers also receive instruction on role definition, maintaining confidentiality, and navigating the development of a connection while maintaining boundaries.
Content of training is delivered through multiple modes such as role-playing scenarios, reviewing case examples, and group discussion.
There are discussions through training to ensure safety for the peer support worker and participant.
For example, when to seek additional support or how to address an uncomfortable situation (e.g., how to create conversations).
Peer support workers are taught procedures for documenting sessions and maintaining fidelity to the intervention, while still allowing flexibility to respond to individual participant needs.
See Appendices A and B for the fidelity checklist and description of session content.

Participants receiving peer support within the PAIR intervention are adults living with ABI who are within one year post-injury and are transitioning from hospital-based rehabilitation to community living.
This timeframe was selected due to the increased need for psychosocial support and life re-construction.

Participants need to have the cognitive and behavioural ability to engage in peer support (with or without communication aids), the ability to participate in a conversation even for short periods, express preferences or goals (verbally, nonverbally, or with support), and regulate behaviour to engage respectfully and safely in one-on-one interactions.
For instance, participants can experience memory challenges, but would be appropriate for PAIR if they are able to retain key information with repetition or external supports.
Additionally, individuals with communication impairments such as aphasia can engage in PAIR if they can use adapted strategies (e.g., visual supports, communication devices, communication partner).
Participants are excluded if they were involved in other structured peer support programs.

Additional screening considerations, such as behavioural stability and readiness to engage in peer support, were applied pragmatically through clinical assessment by the collaborators to ensure participant safety and appropriateness for the intervention.

As such, PAIR is designed to accommodate heterogeneity in ABI experiences, with flexibility in pacing, content, and delivery to support meaningful engagement across a range of functional abilities and life contexts.
The PAIR Research Coordinator is part of the research team and has a central role in the day-to-day management of the intervention.
They have training in accessible communication with people with disability, administration, research tools, and project management.
The PAIR Research Coordinator is responsible for scheduling peer support sessions, data management, and ensuring that study procedures are delivered consistently and according to protocol.
The PAIR Research Coordinator manages the informed consent process and monitors participant engagement and retention throughout the study.
They are responsible for overseeing intervention fidelity, including coordinating session recordings and maintaining documentation.
This role serves as a primary point of contact for troubleshooting logistical or participant-related concerns.
The Research Coordinator oversees research assistants who may assist with PAIR for duties such as recruitment, consent, data collection, and fidelity monitoring.
The PAIR Community Facilitator has a central role in providing oversight and encouragement for the peer support workers.

The person selected for this role has extensive experience working within community-based brain injury services and with people with disabilities; they also have lived experience as a caregiver of a child with an ABI.
In past roles, they developed expertise in facilitating peer connections through the community brain injury peer support program (Nanaimo Brain Injury Society).

The role of the Community Facilitator is to oversee the peer support workers in their role, such as meeting regularly with peer support workers (e.g., at least three times during the twelveweek session) to provide practical guidance and emotional support to facilitate confidence in the peer support worker.
The Community Facilitator debriefs experiences, addresses challenges, and reinforces key principles of PAIR.

In addition, the Community Facilitator supports the research team to ensure that the intervention remains grounded in the realities of living with ABI through adapting communication and study protocols.
Multiple research trainees are involved in this project and are responsible for components of PAIR with corresponding research studies supervised by the Principal Investigator.
For example, one trainee oversees the implementation study including participant recruitment, data collection, and fidelity of intervention.
Another trainee is responsible for data collection on the peer support workers.
Yet another trainee oversees the involvement of the caregiver participants within PAIR as well as supporting the implementation of PAIR.
During the initial design and feasibility testing of PAIR, trainees were also involved.

For example, JG led the initial co-creation and feasibility of PAIR, JG and JW provided insight into the health outcomes measures used in the implementation study, and JG helped to develop accessible materials to support participation in PAIR.
During the delivery of PAIR, trainees are responsible for data collection, intervention implementation, and data management and analysis.
They also lead research team meetings and peer support worker meetings to foster connection, relationship, and best-practices within the implementation process.
Throughout their involvement, trainees gain experience in person-centred and co-created research approaches, while contributing to the rigorous and ethical conduct of the study.
PAIR is delivered through synchronous, individual interactions.

Sessions were planned to occur virtually through secured videoconference, but could be conducted in alternate modalities (e.g., telephone, in-person) depending on participant preference, accessibility, and contextual constraints.
Flexibility in delivery mode is a core feature to support inclusion and access.
PAIR is embedded within community settings.
Recruitment is initiated as participants are preparing for discharge from hospital settings, or shortly after returning home.
This design supports continuity of health services beyond the health institutes.
We first initiated PAIR within the rehabilitation hospital associated with our university and the hospital that we initially partnered with (Nanaimo Regional General Hospital).
We then expanded to six hospitals which are across four out of five provincial health authorities.
PAIR is delivered over 12 weeks, with one session per week.
However, depending on participant needs, schedules, and goals, the dose and duration can be adapted at any point during the intervention.
Session duration is up to 60 minutes, and also tailored to participant needs (e.g., can be reduced in length if participants are fatigued or have reduced attention).
Typically, when a match between a participant and peer support worker is made, they meet at a consistent day and time each week for 12 weeks.

The dose and duration of PAIR was determined through observation of existing peer support programs (e.g., Nanaimo Brain Injury Society), previous research [9 -11], and discussion with people with lived experience and community partners of existing programs.

text.text: As described above in Intervention Procedures, PAIR adheres to core principles of peer support and aligns to Peer Support Canada Competencies.
PAIR is intentionally individualized and continually adapted based on participant needs and goals.
On an individual level, peer support workers respond and adapt conversations based on participant issues in the moment.

While the core relational and theoretical elements remain consistent, the intervention is designed to accommodate heterogeneity in postinjury challenges and personal context, as is often seen in this population [28, 29].

text.text: We conceptualize fidelity in PAIR as adherence to core principles of peer support, rather than particular session content delivered in uniform patterns.
PAIR supports fidelity through standardized training, use of a procedure manual, reflective documentation, and ongoing mentorship and discussion with peer support workers.
A fidelity checklist is completed by peer support workers after each session, encouraging them to reflect on their session and the content of the conversation.
The fidelity checklist also includes an open-ended text box for the peer support worker to indicate issues within the session or notes to be followed up.
To assess intervention fidelity, 20% of all sessions are audio-recorded, as per previous research [30, 31].
text.formatted: To assess intervention fidelity, 20% of all sessions are audio-recorded, as per previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">31]</ref>.

text.text: A member of the research team with no previous connection or relationship to participants or peer support workers independently reviews these recordings and evaluates adherence to the intervention using the standardized fidelity checklist.

In terms of monitoring, the PAIR Community Facilitator meets with peer support workers to understand their lived experience of ABI, their capacity for peer support, personal interests and leisure activities, and relevant cultural or social factors.
This conversation occurs after receiving training and prior to conducting the intervention, helping to inform the matching processes.
Once matched, the PAIR Community Facilitator meets with peer support workers at three occasions during the intervention: after the first session, after the sixth session, and after the tenth session.

These meetings aim to provide support, direction, and encouragement to the peer support worker, discuss steps to manage the completion of the sessions (for the last meeting) and build sustainability for future peer support engagements.
The research team also meets regularly with implementation partners to support intervention delivery, monitor fidelity, and address challenges.

These meetings include regular meetings with hospital collaborators approximately every six weeks to discuss recruitment, referrals, and participant flow; monthly meetings with peer support workers to provide ongoing support, facilitate shared learning, and identify training needs; and quarterly meetings (four per year) with community partners to review implementation experiences, discuss opportunities for program improvement, and support sustainability and integration within local service systems.
This paper describes Peers Actively Involved in Rehabilitation (PAIR), a peer support program for people with ABI; it outlines the development, theoretical foundations, and delivery.
Given the growing calls for improved reporting of complex rehabilitation interventions [32], this paper contributes practical guidance for replication and implementation.

text.text: This paper provides a comprehensive intervention description aligned with TIDieR and informed by GUIDED principles.
As such, this paper supports replication, adaptation, and broader implementation of PAIR across diverse service contexts.

It also contributes to the growing evidence base on the development of peer support interventions by increasing transparency around the theoretical, participatory, and practical processes that shaped the intervention and its delivery.

Notably, previous reviews of peer support interventions for people with ABI have identified a small and heterogeneous evidence base, with considerable variation in intervention characteristics and limited standardization across programs, making it difficult to compare, replicate, and scale interventions across settings [33].

text.text: Detailed reporting of intervention content, delivery procedures, training, and implementation processes may help address these limitations and facilitate the translation of effective peer support programs into routine practice.
PAIR is aligned with previous published evidence on peer support interventions for people living with chronic neurological conditions [9,11].

As key tenants, PAIR, along with other peer support interventions, highlights the importance of lived experience as a guiding principle and focus on psychosocial outcomes rather than impairment remediation [9].

text.text: PAIR builds on previously reported interventions by integrating structured training, tailored procedures, and scaling to multiple sites.
As such, PAIR addresses concerns from previous systematic reviews and qualitative studies [7] [8] [9] 11] by preparing the peer support worker and maintaining high quality assurance of the program.

text.text: Historically, rehabilitation has been grounded in biomedical and expert-led frameworks in which clinicians assess deficits, set goals, and direct intervention [34].

text.text: This often positions patients as passive recipients of care.

While this model has contributed to important advances in clinical outcomes, it has been increasingly critiqued for its limited attention to the lived experience of individuals, the social context of disability, and the importance of autonomy, identity, and meaning in recovery [34, 36].

text.text: In response, contemporary approaches consider social participation, personal meaning, lived experience, and community inclusion in the design and delivery of rehabilitation programs.
There is an emphasis on collaborative partnerships, lived experience, and person-defined goals [35, 37].

text.text: Peer support aligns with contemporary approaches by positioning peer support workers, who are people living with ABI, as experts by experience [8, 9].

text.text: Peer support workers offer unique forms of understanding, validation, and role modeling that are often inaccessible within traditional clinician-led approaches.
Through the reciprocal exchange experience, peer relationships can help normalize daily challenges, reduce feelings of stigma, and improve self-efficacy of those receiving support [11, 15].

Conclusion PAIR demonstrates how peer support can be structured and embedded within community systems while remaining responsive to the heterogeneity of ABI experiences.
PAIR emphasises lived experience, expertise, and co-creation throughout development and delivery.
The intervention aligns with rehabilitation priorities and provides a practical foundation for future implementation, adaptation, and evaluation of peer-led interventions in community-based ABI care.
